d.caption: **The count is the easy argument and the ownership is the real one.** In the left column the agent team writes a binding to a system it does not understand, and the binding rots when that system changes without telling anyone. d.title: Three roles, three process ids, and two independent servers
d.caption: **The pids settle two things people assume otherwise.** Host and server are different processes — over stdio the server is a subprocess the host launched, which makes connecting the same trust decision as installing a dependency. And the second session's call counter starts at 1 again, so each connection is its own server instance: **anything a server holds in memory is per-connection**, including a cache, a counter or an open database handle.

d.title: What the specification defines, and what it hands you
d.caption: **The right-hand column is longer than people expect on first contact**, and two of its rows cause most production trouble. Nothing in the protocol authorises anything, so a server offering `delete_customer` will run it for any client that connects. And nothing in the protocol makes your descriptions good — a model choosing between eleven tools is reading prose you wrote, and that prose is the whole of its routing information.

d.title: Five things MCP does not do for you
d.caption: **Each of these is routinely assumed and none of it is true.** The first is the most common surprise: a server acts with its own credentials, so two different people asking your agent a question arrive at the server as the same caller — per-user answers need identity passed deliberately on top of the protocol. **And the third is the one that makes agents worse rather than merely unsafe:** connecting servers because they are available adds declarations, and tool-choice accuracy falls as the list grows.

d.title: One round trip, five things settled
d.caption: **Capabilities flow both ways, which is the half most summaries omit** — the client declares whether it supports sampling, roots and elicitation, and a server that wants to ask the user something needs the client to have said yes. Note what the version field is worth: `1.28.1` is the SDK's number, and since `FastMCP` has no `version` parameter, every server built on that SDK reports it.

d.title: Every flag is a promise, and omitting one restricts your callers
d.caption: **All three `listChanged` flags came back False, which is the honest answer** for a server that registers its tools at import time and never changes them. **Declaring `listChanged=True` and never sending the notification is worse than leaving it off:** a client that trusted the flag caches the list for the whole connection and has no reason to re-check, so a tool added an hour later is invisible to it — and nothing errors, so the symptom is a model that cannot use a tool plainly present in your source.

d.title: instructions describes the server; a tool description describes one operation
d.caption: **So it is the right home for what no schema can say:** how fresh the data is, what it must not be used for, and a convention that holds across every tool. Two things follow from the host putting that string into a model's context. **It is a hint rather than a control** — a host may ignore, truncate or merely display it, so no rule you depend on can live there. **And from the consumer's side it is someone else's prose entering your prompt**, which makes the handshake an injection surface before a single tool has been called.

d.title: A revision mismatch should fail loudly, at initialize
d.caption: **The expensive outcome is a connection that proceeds hopefully and breaks halfway through a tool call**, where the error surfaces far from its cause and reads like a bug in your own code. Failing at `initialize` is cheap and legible. **And pin the SDK rather than the revision:** a server upgraded across an SDK major can change the revision it offers with no change to your code, which is exactly the kind of movement a handshake log line catches.

d.title: The one handshake field the decorator API cannot set
d.caption: **`FastMCP.__init__` has no `version` parameter** — checked against the installed SDK — while the low-level `Server` has taken one all along. FastMCP builds that server internally without passing it through, so every FastMCP server reports the version of the `mcp` package it was built against. **Assigning to the private `_mcp_server.version` works and the client sees it**, at the price of depending on an underscore attribute an SDK upgrade is entitled to break.

d.title: Who decides - and the model turn that answer costs
d.caption: **The specification's own distinction is one word each, and the cost column is why it matters.** A rate table behind a tool means a declaration the model must consider, a call it must decide to emit, and a second invocation carrying the result: two model turns to obtain a string the host could have read before the conversation opened. **The rule that falls out is short — if the answer does not depend on what the model is thinking, it is not a tool.**

d.title: Templates come back from a different call
d.caption: **`list_resources` returned only the concrete `rates://current`.** The parameterised `vat://{country}` is in `list_resource_templates`, because a template cannot be read until a parameter is supplied — which is the point of templates, since it lets a server describe the shape of an address without enumerating ten thousand instances. **A client that only calls `list_resources` is blind to all of them**, so if you expect a host to discover a template, check that it asks.

d.title: Four rules for a resource, and the one with teeth
d.caption: **Nothing in the protocol stops a read from doing work, and nothing promises how often a host will call it — and those two facts combine badly.** A host that pre-fetches every listed resource when a conversation opens is behaving correctly, so a read that increments a counter or sends a notification will fire on connections where nobody asked for anything. The discipline is one line: **a read answers what the value is; anything answering do this is a tool.**

d.caption: **Three of these rows put text in front of a model and hope; the last one is enforceable.** That is the sentence to carry out of the lesson. d.title: Host support decides whether a correct design does anything
d.caption: **This is why servers drift towards tool-only designs, and it is rational rather than lazy:** a tool is the one primitive guaranteed to be used. The pragmatic shape is to model everything correctly and expose the one or two important read-only items twice — one function, two decorators — so a well-built host gets the efficient path and a tool-only host still works. **Do not do it for everything**, because each extra tool is a declaration in every request and a candidate for mis-selection.
